findings.title: Possible brute-force or credential stuffing
evidence: 1 address made 70 authentication attempts (401/403 responses or login POSTs)
198.51.100.203: 70 attempts within one 5-minute window (0 denied, 70 login POSTs, 70 in total), 2026-11-12T09:36:03Z to 2026-11-12T09:39:30Z
limitations: Counts 401 responses and POSTs to login-like URLs per address inside one aligned 5-minute window; slow attacks and distributed attacks (one try per address) are not detected.
Clients behind NAT or a shared proxy are merged, and monitoring probes with a bad credential look like brute force.
Many login POSTs do not mean failures: successful logins are counted too.

findings.title: Command or code injection signatures
evidence: 1 matching request from 1 address between 2026-11-12T21:22:18Z and 2026-11-12T21:22:18Z
limitations: Heuristic: an access log shows requests, not their effect. A match is an attempt, not proof of compromise.
Matches shell, PHP and Java-classloader syntax in the URL and Shellshock in the user agent or referer; payloads in other headers or bodies are not visible.
Query strings that carry code snippets (a coding tutorial site, for example) can match.

findings.title: Log4Shell (JNDI lookup) attempts
evidence: 3 matching requests from 1 address between 2026-11-13T07:26:24Z and 2026-11-13T07:26:30Z
1 of these request was answered with a 2xx status, for example GET / [200]
limitations: Heuristic: an access log shows requests, not their effect. A match is an attempt, not proof of compromise.
Detects ${jndi:...} lookups (including common obfuscations) in the URL, user agent and referer only; other headers are not logged by default.
Whether the lookup worked depends on your Java dependencies, not on this log.

findings.title: Path traversal or local file inclusion attempts
evidence: 8 matching requests from 1 address between 2026-11-12T21:21:43Z and 2026-11-12T21:22:32Z
1 of these request was answered with a 2xx status, for example GET /download?file=../../../etc/passwd [200]
limitations: Heuristic: an access log shows requests, not their effect. A match is an attempt, not proof of compromise.
Only the request target (path and query, first 2 KiB, decoded twice) is inspected; headers and request bodies are not in the log.
Legitimate URLs rarely contain system file names, but documentation sites can.

findings.title: SQL injection signatures in URLs
evidence: 60 matching requests from 1 address between 2026-11-11T16:48:04Z and 2026-11-11T16:52:00Z
sample: GET /api/v1/products?id=1 UNION SELECT username,password FROM users [200]
54 of these requests were answered with a 2xx status, for example GET /api/v1/products?id=1%27 AND 1=1-- [200]
limitations: Heuristic: an access log shows requests, not their effect. A match is an attempt, not proof of compromise.
Signature matching on the decoded URL: obfuscated payloads and POST-body injections are invisible to an access log.
Site-search boxes can legitimately contain SQL words (someone searching for 'union select').

findings.title: Probing for sensitive or admin paths
evidence: 42 probe requests from 1 address between 2026-11-10T15:36:02Z and 2026-11-10T15:37:30Z
categories: framework-debug 9, cms-admin 7, cgi-iot 6, env-files 4, vcs 4, backup-files 3, credentials 3, db-admin 3
limitations: Name-based matching: a site that really serves these paths (for example WordPress admin pages) produces matches, so only clients that trigger several different probe rules, or any sensitive file, are reported.
A 2xx answer does not prove exposure: single-page apps and catch-all routes answer every path with 200. Check the response body.
Clients are tracked in bounded memory; low-volume scanners can be evicted on very busy logs.

findings.title: Security scanners identified by user agent
evidence: 105 matching requests from 2 addresses between 2026-11-10T15:36:02Z and 2026-11-11T16:52:00Z
54 of these requests were answered with a 2xx status, for example GET /api/v1/products?id=1%27 AND 1=1-- [200]
limitations: User agents are self-reported: scanners that pose as browsers are missed.
Some matches are legitimate internet-wide research scanners, which are noisy but not necessarily hostile.

findings.title: Clients with outlier request rates
evidence: 1 client sent at least 60 requests in a single minute; the typical busiest minute of the 210 tracked clients is 1
192.0.2.207: up to 207 requests in one minute (520 in total)
limitations: Request rate only: CDNs, NAT gateways, monitoring and reverse proxies legitimately produce high rates.
If every request shares one address you are probably logging a proxy's address instead of the client's; fix the log format or use X-Forwarded-For first.
Only the busiest tracked clients are compared and per-minute peaks assume mostly chronological logs.

findings.title: Cross-site scripting signatures in URLs
evidence: 6 matching requests from 1 address between 2026-11-13T14:09:41Z and 2026-11-13T14:10:06Z
6 of these requests were answered with a 2xx status, for example GET /api/v1/search?q=%3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C/script%3E [200]
limitations: Heuristic: an access log shows requests, not their effect. A match is an attempt, not proof of compromise.
Only the URL is inspected; stored or POST-body XSS cannot be seen in an access log.
Developers testing their own site and security scanners produce the same patterns.
